nodes.name: Space of symmetric matrices $\mathbb{S}^n$ with the Frobenius inner product
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{S}^n$ denote the space of symmetric real $n \times n$ matrices, equipped with the Frobenius inner product $\langle X,Y\rangle_F:=\mathrm{tr}(XY)$ and its induced norm $\|\cdot\|_F$.

nodes.name: Positive definite and positive semidefinite cones
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{S}^n_{++} \subset \mathbb{S}^n$ be the (open) cone of positive-definite matrices, and let $\mathbb{S}^n_{+} \subset \mathbb{S}^n$ be the (closed) cone of positive semidefinite matrices.

nodes.name: Orthogonal complement ${\mathcal{S}}^\perp$ of a subspace
nodes.statement: A linear subspace ${\mathcal{S}}\subset\mathbb{S}^n$ has orthogonal complement ${\mathcal{S}}^\perp := \{\,X\in\mathbb{S}^n:\ \mathrm{tr}(XY)=0\ \ \forall\,Y\in {\mathcal{S}}\,\}$.

nodes.name: General structured decomposition
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathcal{S}}\subset\mathbb{S}^n$ be a linear subspace. \begin{enumerate} \item[\textbf{(i)}] If ${\mathcal{S}}$ contains no nonzero positive semidefinite matrix, that is, \begin{equation} {\mathcal{S}} \cap \mathbb{S}^n_{+} = \{0\}, \end{equation} then every $A\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$ admits a \emph{unique} pair $(B^\ast \in \mathbb{S}^n_{++} \cap {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}, C^\ast \in {\mathcal{S}})$ such that \begin{equation} A = {B^\ast}^{-1} + C^\ast. \end{equation} \item[\textbf{(ii)}] Conversely, if \eqref{eq:maindecomposition} admits a solution for even a single $A\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$, then \eqref{eq:nopsddirections} holds. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Boundedness of the feasible set $\Omega_C$
nodes.statement: Let $A \in \mathbb{S}_{++}^n$ and let ${\mathcal{S}} \subset \mathbb{S}^n$ be a linear subspace satisfying \eqref{eq:nopsddirections}. Define the feasible set \begin{equation} \Omega_C := \{\, C \in {\mathcal{S}} : A - C \succ 0 \,\}. \end{equation} Then $\Omega_C$ is a bounded subset of ${\mathcal{S}}$. In particular, its closure $\overline{\Omega_C}$ is compact.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (bounded feasible set)
nodes.statement: Assume by contradiction that $\Omega_C$ is unbounded. Then there exists a sequence $\{C^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{\infty} \subset \Omega_C$ with $\|C^{(k)}\|_F \underset{k \to \infty}{\longrightarrow} \infty$, where $|| \cdot ||_F$ is the Frobenius norm. Define the normalized matrices \begin{equation} X^{(k)} := \frac{C^{(k)}}{\|C^{(k)}\|_F} \in {\mathcal{S}}. \end{equation} Since $\|X^{(k)}\|_F = 1$, the sequence $\{X^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{\infty}$ lies in a compact set, and therefore it has a converging subsequence $\{X^{(k_j)}\}_{j=1}^{\infty}$ with $X^{(k_j)} \underset{j \to \infty}{\longrightarrow} X$ for some $X \in {\mathcal{S}}$ with $\|X\|_F = 1$. Take the corresponding subsequence $\{C^{(k_j)}\}_{j=1}^{\infty}$ of $\{C^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{\infty}$. The condition $A - C^{(k_j)} \succ 0$ yields for every fixed nonzero vector $v \in \mathbb{R}^n$, \begin{equation} \frac{v^{\top} C^{(k_j)} v}{\|C^{(k_j)}\|_F} < \frac{v^{\top} A v}{\|C^{(k_j)}\|_F} \underset{j \to \infty}{\longrightarrow} 0, \end{equation} where the limit on the right-hand side follows from the assumption that $\|C^{(k)}\|_F \underset{k \to \infty}{\longrightarrow} \infty$. But continuity of quadratic forms yields \begin{equation} \frac{v^{\top} C^{(k_j)} v}{\|C^{(k_j)}\|_F} \; \underset{j \to \infty}{\longrightarrow} \; v^{\top} X v . \end{equation} Hence $v^{\top} X v \le 0$ for all $v \in \mathbb{R}^n$. Thus, $X \preceq 0$. But $X\neq 0$ and $X \in {\mathcal{S}}$, and so $-X \in {\mathcal{S}}$ satisfies $-X \succeq 0$, in contradiction to ${\mathcal{S}} \cap \mathbb{S}^n_{+} = \{0\}$. Therefore $\Omega_C$ must be bounded.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: normalize an unbounded sequence, extract a limit $X\in{\mathcal{S}}$ with $X\preceq0$, so $-X$ is a nonzero PSD element of ${\mathcal{S}}$.

nodes.name: Step 1: reduce the decomposition to a stationarity condition
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 1: Reduction of the decomposition to a stationarity condition.} Let $D_1,...,D_m\in {\mathcal{S}}$ be a basis for ${\mathcal{S}}$. Define the linear bijection \begin{equation} C(x) := \sum_{k=1}^m x_k D_k , \qquad x \in \mathbb{R}^m, \end{equation} and the corresponding feasible parameter set \begin{equation} \Omega_x := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^m : A - C(x) \succ 0 \,\}. \end{equation} Hence the feasible set of matrices $\Omega_C$ defined in eq. \eqref{eq:feasible_matrices} satisfies $\Omega_C = C(\Omega_x)$. For $x \in \Omega_x$ let \begin{equation} M(x) := A - C(x), \qquad B(x) := M(x)^{-1}, \qquad \Phi(x) := -\log\det\bigl(M(x)\bigr). \end{equation} Using the chain rule for $M$ and $-\log\det(\cdot)$ we obtain \begin{equation} \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial x_k}(x) = \mathrm{tr} \big( B(x) D_k \big), \qquad k = 1,\dots,m. \end{equation} Thus a pair $(B,C)\in \mathbb{S}^n_{++} \times {\mathcal{S}}$ with $A=B^{-1}+C$ and $\mathrm{tr}(BD_k)=0$ for all $k$ corresponds precisely to a parameter $x$ such that $C=C(x)$ and \begin{equation} \nabla\Phi(x)=0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Step 1: reduce the decomposition to a stationarity condition of $\Phi$

nodes.name: Step 2: existence and uniqueness of the minimizer
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 2: Existence and uniqueness of a minimizer.} The map $M(x)$ is affine and injective, and $-\log\det(\cdot)$ is strictly convex on $\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$, hence $\Phi$ is strictly convex on the convex set $\Omega_x$. If a sequence $\{x^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{\infty}$ approaches $\partial\Omega_x$, then along a subsequence $x^{(k)}\to\bar x\in\partial\Omega_x$, so that $M(x^{(k)})\to M(\bar x)\succeq0$ with $M(\bar x)$ singular; hence $\det\bigl(M(x^{(k)})\bigr) \to 0$ and $\Phi(x^{(k)}) \to +\infty$ as $k \to \infty$. Since $A \succ 0$ and $C(0)=0$, we have $0 \in \Omega_x$ and $\Omega_x$ is nonempty. By Lemma~\ref{lem:bounded_intersection}, the set $\Omega_C$ is bounded. Thus $\Omega_x = C^{-1}(\Omega_C)$ is bounded as well, and $\overline{\Omega_x}$ is compact. Extend $\Phi$ to $\overline{\Omega_x}$ by setting $\Phi = +\infty$ on $\partial\Omega_x$. Lower semicontinuity of $\Phi$ and compactness of $\overline{\Omega_x}$ yield a minimizer $x^\ast \in \Omega_x$, and strict convexity implies that $x^\ast$ is unique. Since $\Phi$ is differentiable and strictly convex on the open set $\Omega_x$, any stationary point is the global minimizer. Thus the unique minimizer $x^\ast$ is also the unique point in $\Omega_x$ satisfying $\nabla\Phi(x^\ast)=0$. Define $C^\ast := C(x^\ast)$ and $B^\ast := (A - C^\ast)^{-1}$. Then the pair $(B^\ast,C^\ast) \in \mathbb{S}^n_{++} \times {\mathcal{S}}$ satisfies \eqref{eq:maindecomposition}. Uniqueness of $x^\ast$ and the equivalence in Step~1 imply the uniqueness of the decomposition \eqref{eq:maindecomposition}. This proves part~\textbf{(i)}.
nodes.statement_short: Step 2: existence and uniqueness of the minimizer

nodes.name: Sufficient condition and variational necessity of nondegeneracy
nodes.statement: A sufficient condition for \eqref{eq:nopsddirections} is the existence of a matrix $\hat B \in \mathbb{S}^n_{++}$ such that \[ \mathrm{tr}(\hat B X) = 0, \ \forall X\in {\mathcal{S}}. \] Part~\textbf{(ii)} of Theorem~\ref{thm:general_decomposition} has a variational counterpart, which explains how the construction of Step~2 fails without \eqref{eq:nopsddirections}: the condition is also necessary for a minimizer of $-\log\det(A-C)$ over $\Omega_C$ to exist. Suppose there exists a matrix $X \neq 0$ satisfying $X \in \mathbb{S}^n_{+} \cap {\mathcal{S}}$. Define $C_t = -tX$. Then $A-C_t = A + tX \succ 0$ for all $t \geq 0$, hence the feasible set $\Omega_C$ is unbounded. Therefore, $\det(A-C_t) \underset{t \to \infty}{\longrightarrow} \infty$ hence the objective $-\log\det(A-C_t)$ is unbounded below.
nodes.statement_short: A positive definite $\hat B\perp{\mathcal{S}}$ suffices for nondegeneracy; without it the log-det objective is unbounded below along $-tX$.
nodes.label: remark1

nodes.name: Primal log-determinant characterization of $C^*$
nodes.statement: By Step~2 of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:general_decomposition}, the matrix $C^\ast$ is the unique minimizer of the strictly convex problem \begin{equation} \min_{C\in\Omega_C} \; -\log\det(A-C) . \end{equation}
conclusions: the matrix $C^\ast$ is the unique minimizer of the strictly convex problem \begin{equation} \min_{C\in\Omega_C} \; -\log\det(A-C) . \end{equation}

nodes.name: Primal log-det problem
nodes.statement: \min_{C\in\Omega_C} \; -\log\det(A-C) .
nodes.label: eq:primal_logdet

nodes.name: Derivation of the dual log-determinant problem
nodes.statement: The primal problem \eqref{eq:primal_logdet} can be written as minimizing $-\log\det(M)$ over $M\succ0$ subject to the linear constraint $A-M\in {\mathcal{S}}$, where $M=A-C$ is an auxiliary variable. The associated Lagrangian involves a dual variable $B\in {\mathcal{S}}^\perp$. Eliminating $M$ via the first-order optimality condition $M^{-1}=B$ yields the dual problem stated below: Let $(B^\ast \in \mathbb{S}^n_{++} \cap {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp},\, C^\ast \in {\mathcal{S}})$ be the unique pair satisfying \eqref{eq:maindecomposition}. For any $B \in {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ and $C \in {\mathcal{S}}$ we have $\mathrm{tr}(B C) = 0$ hence $\mathrm{tr} \big( (A-C)B \big)=\mathrm{tr}(BA)$. The function \[ \Psi_A(B):= \log\det(B)-\mathrm{tr}(BA)+n, \qquad B\in \mathbb{S}^n_{++} \cap {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}, \] is strictly concave and satisfies the first-order optimality condition \[ \nabla\Psi_A(B^\ast) = {B^\ast}^{-1}-A \quad ; \quad \mathrm{tr}\!\big(( {B^\ast}^{-1}-A )X\big)=0 \:,\: \forall X\in {\mathcal{S}}^\perp . \] Moreover, using the decomposition $A={B^\ast}^{-1}+C^\ast$ with $C^\ast\in {\mathcal{S}}$, we have for every $X\in {\mathcal{S}}^\perp$, \[ \mathrm{tr}\big( ({B^\ast}^{-1}-A) X \big) = -\mathrm{tr}(C^\ast X)=0 . \] Hence $B^\ast$ satisfies the first-order optimality conditions for $\Psi_A$.
nodes.statement_short: Lagrangian duality: eliminate $M=A-C$ to get the concave dual $\Psi_A$, and check that $B^*$ satisfies its first-order conditions using $A=(B^*)^{-1}+C^*$.

nodes.name: Rewrite with $M=A-C$
nodes.statement: The primal problem \eqref{eq:primal_logdet} can be written as minimizing $-\log\det(M)$ over $M\succ0$ subject to the linear constraint $A-M\in {\mathcal{S}}$, where $M=A-C$ is an auxiliary variable. The associated Lagrangian involves a dual variable $B\in {\mathcal{S}}^\perp$. Eliminating $M$ via the first-order optimality condition $M^{-1}=B$ yields the dual problem stated below:
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite with $M=A-C$; Lagrange multiplier $B\in{\mathcal{S}}^\perp$; eliminate $M$

nodes.name: Orthogonality gives $\mathrm{tr}((A-C)B)=\mathrm{tr}(BA)$
nodes.statement: Let $(B^\ast \in \mathbb{S}^n_{++} \cap {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp},\, C^\ast \in {\mathcal{S}})$ be the unique pair satisfying \eqref{eq:maindecomposition}. For any $B \in {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}$ and $C \in {\mathcal{S}}$ we have $\mathrm{tr}(B C) = 0$ hence $\mathrm{tr} \big( (A-C)B \big)=\mathrm{tr}(BA)$.
nodes.statement_short: Orthogonality gives $\mathrm{tr}((A-C)B)=\mathrm{tr}(BA)$

nodes.name: Introduce the concave dual objective $\Psi_A$ and its gradie
nodes.statement: The function \[ \Psi_A(B):= \log\det(B)-\mathrm{tr}(BA)+n, \qquad B\in \mathbb{S}^n_{++} \cap {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}, \] is strictly concave and satisfies the first-order optimality condition \[ \nabla\Psi_A(B^\ast) = {B^\ast}^{-1}-A \quad ; \quad \mathrm{tr}\!\big(( {B^\ast}^{-1}-A )X\big)=0 \:,\: \forall X\in {\mathcal{S}}^\perp . \]
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the concave dual objective $\Psi_A$ and its gradient

nodes.name: $B^*$ satisfies the first-order conditions of $\Psi_A$
nodes.statement: Moreover, using the decomposition $A={B^\ast}^{-1}+C^\ast$ with $C^\ast\in {\mathcal{S}}$, we have for every $X\in {\mathcal{S}}^\perp$, \[ \mathrm{tr}\big( ({B^\ast}^{-1}-A) X \big) = -\mathrm{tr}(C^\ast X)=0 . \] Hence $B^\ast$ satisfies the first-order optimality conditions for $\Psi_A$.
nodes.statement_short: $B^*$ satisfies the first-order conditions of $\Psi_A$

nodes.name: Dual characterization: $B^*$ maximizes the dual log-det problem
nodes.statement: Since $\log\det(B)$ is strictly concave on $\mathbb{S}^n_{++} \cap {\mathcal{S}}^\perp$, we conclude that $B^\ast$ is the unique maximizer of the dual problem \begin{equation} \max_{B\succ 0,\; B\in {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}} \log\det(B)-\mathrm{tr}(BA)+n. \end{equation}
conclusions: $B^\ast$ is the unique maximizer of the dual problem \begin{equation} \max_{B\succ 0,\; B\in {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}} \log\det(B)-\mathrm{tr}(BA)+n. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Dual log-det problem
nodes.statement: \max_{B\succ 0,\; B\in {\mathcal{S}}^{\perp}} \log\det(B)-\mathrm{tr}(BA)+n.
nodes.label: eq:dual_logdet

nodes.name: Strong duality between the primal and dual log-det problems
nodes.statement: Since the primal problem \eqref{eq:primal_logdet} is convex and strictly feasible, strong duality holds, and the primal and dual optimal values coincide.
assumptions: Since the primal problem \eqref{eq:primal_logdet} is convex and strictly feasible,
conclusions: strong duality holds, and the primal and dual optimal values coincide.

nodes.name: Dual problem as an alternative computational route
nodes.statement: Accordingly, the dual problem \eqref{eq:dual_logdet} provides an alternative computational route to the decomposition. One may optimize directly over $B \in {\mathcal{S}}^\perp \cap \mathbb{S}^n_{++}$ using standard iterative methods, including Newton-type schemes with feasibility-preserving backtracking. The primal formulation is preferable when $m=\dim {\mathcal{S}}$ is small, while the dual formulation may be preferable when $\dim({\mathcal{S}}^\perp)$ is comparatively small or when the constraint structure is naturally expressed in terms of $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Optimize over $B$ directly; primal preferable for small $\dim{\mathcal{S}}$, dual for small $\dim{\mathcal{S}}^\perp$.

nodes.name: Orthogonal group ${\mathcal{O}}(n)$
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathcal{O}}(n)$ denote the set of all $n \times n$ orthogonal matrices.

nodes.name: Action by conjugation
nodes.statement: For $P \in {\mathcal{O}}(n)$, consider the action on $\mathbb{S}^n$ by conjugation, $X \mapsto P X P^\top$ ($P^\top$ denotes transposition).

nodes.name: Equivariance of the decomposition under orthogonal conjugation
nodes.statement: From the equality \[ \mathrm{tr}\!\left(P B^\ast P^\top \, P X P^\top\right) = \mathrm{tr}(B^\ast X) = 0 \:, \qquad \forall X \in {\mathcal{S}}, \] we conclude that \[ P A P^\top = (P B^\ast P^\top)^{-1} + P C^\ast P^\top \] is the unique decomposition \eqref{eq:maindecomposition} of $P A P^\top$ associated with the subspace $ \tilde {\mathcal{S}} := P {\mathcal{S}} P^\top . $
conclusions: P A P^\top = (P B^\ast P^\top)^{-1} + P C^\ast P^\top \] is the unique decomposition \eqref{eq:maindecomposition} of $P A P^\top$ associated with the subspace $ \tilde {\mathcal{S}} := P {\mathcal{S}} P^\top . $
nodes.statement_short: Conjugating $A$ and ${\mathcal{S}}$ by an orthogonal $P$ conjugates both components of the decomposition.

nodes.name: Group $\mathcal G$ acting by conjugation
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal G \subset {\mathcal{O}}(n)$ act on $\mathbb{S}^n$ by conjugation, $ X \mapsto P X P^\top . $

nodes.name: $\mathcal G$-fixed matrix and $\mathcal G$-invariant subspace
nodes.statement: Assume that $A$ is $\mathcal G$-fixed, i.e., $ PA P^\top = A \quad \forall P \in \mathcal G, $ and that ${\mathcal{S}}$ is $\mathcal G$-invariant, i.e., $ P {\mathcal{S}} P^\top = {\mathcal{S}} \quad \forall P \in \mathcal G. $

nodes.name: Inheritance of group symmetry
nodes.statement: By the above analysis and the uniqueness of the decomposition \eqref{eq:maindecomposition}, the decomposition is then $\mathcal G$-fixed: \begin{equation} P B^\ast P^\top = B^\ast, \qquad P C^\ast P^\top = C^\ast, \quad \forall P \in \mathcal G. \end{equation}
conclusions: the decomposition is then $\mathcal G$-fixed:
nodes.statement_short: If $A$ is $\mathcal G$-fixed and ${\mathcal{S}}$ is $\mathcal G$-invariant then $B^*$ and $C^*$ are $\mathcal G$-fixed.

nodes.name: $\mathcal G$-fixedness of $B^*$ and $C^*$
nodes.statement: P B^\ast P^\top = B^\ast, \qquad P C^\ast P^\top = C^\ast, \quad \forall P \in \mathcal G.
nodes.label: eq:G_fixed

nodes.name: Determinant inequality $\det(B^*)\le\det(A^{-1})$
nodes.statement: From the primal representation, \[ -\log\det(A) = -\log\det(A-0) \;\ge\; -\log\det(A-C^\ast), \] where the inequality follows from optimality of $C^\ast$. Hence \[ -\log\det(A) \ge -\log\det({B^\ast}^{-1}), \] which implies \begin{equation} \det({B^\ast}^{-1}) \ge \det(A), \quad\text{i.e.}\quad \det(B^\ast) \le \det(A^{-1}). \end{equation}
conclusions: \det({B^\ast}^{-1}) \ge \det(A), \quad\text{i.e.}\quad \det(B^\ast) \le \det(A^{-1}).
nodes.statement_short: Comparing the primal objective at $C=0$ and $C^*$ gives $\det((B^*)^{-1})\ge\det(A)$.

nodes.name: Determinant inequality
nodes.statement: \det({B^\ast}^{-1}) \ge \det(A), \quad\text{i.e.}\quad \det(B^\ast) \le \det(A^{-1}).
nodes.label: eq:det_ineq

nodes.name: Decomposition of the inverse $A^{-1}$
nodes.statement: Define the transformed subspace \[ \hat {\mathcal{S}} := A^{-1} {\mathcal{S}} A^{-1} = \{\, A^{-1} X A^{-1} : X \in {\mathcal{S}} \,\} \subset \mathbb{S}^n, \] and set \begin{equation} \hat B := A B^\ast A, \qquad \hat C := A^{-1} C^\ast A^{-1}. \end{equation} Then, for all \(X \in {\mathcal{S}}\), \[ \mathrm{tr}(\hat B\, A^{-1} X A^{-1}) = \mathrm{tr}(B^\ast X) = 0. \] Consequently, \[ \hat B \in \hat {\mathcal{S}}^\perp, \quad \hat B \succ 0, \quad \hat C \in \hat {\mathcal{S}}, \quad A^{-1} = \hat B^{-1} + \hat C. \] The subspace \(\hat {\mathcal{S}}\) inherits \eqref{eq:nopsddirections}: the congruence \(X\mapsto A^{-1}XA^{-1}\) is a linear bijection of \(\mathbb{S}^n\) that preserves positive semidefiniteness in both directions, so a nonzero element of \(\hat {\mathcal{S}}\cap\mathbb{S}^n_{+}\) would produce a nonzero element of \({\mathcal{S}}\cap\mathbb{S}^n_{+}\). By uniqueness of the decomposition \eqref{eq:maindecomposition}, \((\hat B,\hat C) \in \mathbb{S}^n_{++} \times \hat {\mathcal{S}}\) is the unique decomposition of \(A^{-1}\) associated with \(\hat {\mathcal{S}}\).
conclusions: \((\hat B,\hat C) \in \mathbb{S}^n_{++} \times \hat {\mathcal{S}}\) is the unique decomposition of \(A^{-1}\) associated with \(\hat {\mathcal{S}}\).
nodes.statement_short: $A^{-1}=(AB^*A)^{-1}+A^{-1}C^*A^{-1}$ is the decomposition of $A^{-1}$ for $\hat{\mathcal{S}}=A^{-1}{\mathcal{S}}A^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Transformed components $\hat B$, $\hat C$
nodes.statement: \hat B := A B^\ast A, \qquad \hat C := A^{-1} C^\ast A^{-1}.
nodes.label: deco

nodes.name: Decomposition map $A\mapsto(B^*(A),C^*(A))$
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{thm:general_decomposition} each $A\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$ determines a unique pair, which we write $\big(B^{*}(A),C^{*}(A)\big)$.

nodes.name: Nonzero constraint subspace
nodes.statement: Assume throughout that ${\mathcal{S}}\neq\{0\}$ (for ${\mathcal{S}}=\{0\}$ the decomposition is $C^{*}(A)=0$, $B^{*}(A)=A^{-1}$).

nodes.name: Curvature constant $\alpha(B,{\mathcal{S}})$
nodes.statement: For $B\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$ set \begin{equation} \alpha(B,{\mathcal{S}}):=\min_{X\in {\mathcal{S}},\ \|X\|_F=1}\mathrm{tr}(BXBX) , \end{equation} where $\mathrm{tr}(BXBX)$ is the second derivative of $C\mapsto-\log\det(A-C)$ in the direction $X$, at the point $C$ with $B=(A-C)^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha(B,{\mathcal{S}})$ is the minimum of $\mathrm{tr}(BXBX)$ over unit $X\in{\mathcal{S}}$, the minimal curvature of the log-det objective along ${\mathcal{S}}$.

nodes.name: Definition of $\alpha(B,{\mathcal{S}})$
nodes.statement: \alpha(B,{\mathcal{S}}):=\min_{X\in {\mathcal{S}},\ \|X\|_F=1}\mathrm{tr}(BXBX) ,
nodes.label: eq:alpha_def_fro

nodes.name: Positivity and Lipschitz continuity of $\alpha$
nodes.statement: Let $B,B'\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$ and let ${\mathcal{S}}\subset\mathbb{S}^n$ be a nonzero linear subspace. \begin{enumerate} \item[\textbf{(i)}] $0<\lambda_{\min}(B)^2\le\alpha(B,{\mathcal{S}})\le\|B\|_2^2$. \item[\textbf{(ii)}] $\big|\alpha(B',{\mathcal{S}})-\alpha(B,{\mathcal{S}})\big|\le\big(\|B'\|_2+\|B\|_2\big)\,\|B'-B\|_2$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $B,B'\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$ and let ${\mathcal{S}}\subset\mathbb{S}^n$ be a nonzero linear subspace.
conclusions: $0<\lambda_{\min}(B)^2\le\alpha(B,{\mathcal{S}})\le\|B\|_2^2$.
$\big|\alpha(B',{\mathcal{S}})-\alpha(B,{\mathcal{S}})\big|\le\big(\|B'\|_2+\|B\|_2\big)\,\|B'-B\|_2$.
nodes.statement_short: $\lambda_{\min}(B)^2\le\alpha(B,{\mathcal{S}})\le\|B\|_2^2$, and $\alpha$ is Lipschitz in $B$ with constant $\|B'\|_2+\|B\|_2$.
nodes.label: lem:alpha_lipschitz

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (positivity and Lipschitz continuity of $\alpha$)
nodes.statement: \textbf{(i)} For $X\in\mathbb{S}^n$, \begin{align*} \mathrm{tr}(BXBX)&=\|B^{1/2}XB^{1/2}\|_F^2 ,\\ \lambda_{\min}(B)\|X\|_F&\le\|B^{1/2}XB^{1/2}\|_F\le\|B\|_2\|X\|_F . \end{align*} Squaring the second chain and minimizing over $X\in {\mathcal{S}}$ with $\|X\|_F=1$, a compact set, gives the two inequalities, the first strict because $\lambda_{\min}(B)>0$ for $B\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$. \textbf{(ii)} For every $X\in\mathbb{S}^n$, \begin{align*} \big|\mathrm{tr}(B'XB'X)-\mathrm{tr}(BXBX)\big| &=\big|\mathrm{tr}\big((B'-B)XB'X\big)+\mathrm{tr}\big(BX(B'-B)X\big)\big|\\ &\le\|(B'-B)X\|_F\big(\|B'X\|_F+\|BX\|_F\big)\\ &\le\big(\|B'\|_2+\|B\|_2\big)\,\|B'-B\|_2\,\|X\|_F^2 , \end{align*} the second step by the triangle inequality and $|\mathrm{tr}(MN)|\le\|M\|_F\|N\|_F$, the third by $\|MX\|_F\le\|M\|_2\|X\|_F$. At every $X\in{\mathcal{S}}$ with $\|X\|_F=1$ the two traces therefore differ by at most $\big(\|B'\|_2+\|B\|_2\big)\|B'-B\|_2$, hence so do their minima over that set, namely $\alpha(B',{\mathcal{S}})$ and $\alpha(B,{\mathcal{S}})$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\mathrm{tr}(BXBX)=\|B^{1/2}XB^{1/2}\|_F^2$ and bound it; for (ii) expand the difference of traces and use Cauchy-Schwarz.

nodes.name: (i): sandwich $\|B^{1/2}XB^{1/2}\|_F$ between $\lambda_{\min
nodes.statement: \textbf{(i)} For $X\in\mathbb{S}^n$, \begin{align*} \mathrm{tr}(BXBX)&=\|B^{1/2}XB^{1/2}\|_F^2 ,\\ \lambda_{\min}(B)\|X\|_F&\le\|B^{1/2}XB^{1/2}\|_F\le\|B\|_2\|X\|_F . \end{align*} Squaring the second chain and minimizing over $X\in {\mathcal{S}}$ with $\|X\|_F=1$, a compact set, gives the two inequalities, the first strict because $\lambda_{\min}(B)>0$ for $B\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$.
nodes.statement_short: (i): sandwich $\|B^{1/2}XB^{1/2}\|_F$ between $\lambda_{\min}(B)\|X\|_F$ and $\|B\|_2\|X\|_F$

nodes.name: (ii): bound the difference of the traces pointwise, then of
nodes.statement: \textbf{(ii)} For every $X\in\mathbb{S}^n$, \begin{align*} \big|\mathrm{tr}(B'XB'X)-\mathrm{tr}(BXBX)\big| &=\big|\mathrm{tr}\big((B'-B)XB'X\big)+\mathrm{tr}\big(BX(B'-B)X\big)\big|\\ &\le\|(B'-B)X\|_F\big(\|B'X\|_F+\|BX\|_F\big)\\ &\le\big(\|B'\|_2+\|B\|_2\big)\,\|B'-B\|_2\,\|X\|_F^2 , \end{align*} the second step by the triangle inequality and $|\mathrm{tr}(MN)|\le\|M\|_F\|N\|_F$, the third by $\|MX\|_F\le\|M\|_2\|X\|_F$. At every $X\in{\mathcal{S}}$ with $\|X\|_F=1$ the two traces therefore differ by at most $\big(\|B'\|_2+\|B\|_2\big)\|B'-B\|_2$, hence so do their minima over that set, namely $\alpha(B',{\mathcal{S}})$ and $\alpha(B,{\mathcal{S}})$.
nodes.statement_short: (ii): bound the difference of the traces pointwise, then of their minima

nodes.name: Restricted condition number $\kappa(B,{\mathcal{S}})$
nodes.statement: Part~\textbf{(i)} gives $\alpha(B,{\mathcal{S}})>0$, so we may write \begin{equation} \kappa(B,{\mathcal{S}}):=\frac{\|B\|_2}{\sqrt{\alpha(B,{\mathcal{S}})}} \end{equation} for the associated restricted condition number, which satisfies $1\le\kappa(B,{\mathcal{S}})\le\lambda_{\max}(B)/\lambda_{\min}(B)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\kappa(B,{\mathcal{S}})=\|B\|_2/\sqrt{\alpha(B,{\mathcal{S}})}$, between 1 and the condition number of $B$.

nodes.name: Definition of $\kappa(B,{\mathcal{S}})$
nodes.statement: \kappa(B,{\mathcal{S}}):=\frac{\|B\|_2}{\sqrt{\alpha(B,{\mathcal{S}})}}
nodes.label: eq:kappa_def

nodes.name: Local stability of the decomposition
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$ with decomposition $(B^{*},C^{*})$ given by Theorem~\ref{thm:general_decomposition} for a nonzero subspace ${\mathcal{S}}$, and let $\widetilde A=A+\Delta\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$ have decomposition $(\widetilde B,\widetilde C)$ for the same ${\mathcal{S}}$. Set \begin{equation} \varepsilon:=\|B^{*}\|_2\,\kappa(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})^{2}\,\|\Delta\|_F =\frac{\|B^{*}\|_2^{3}\,\|\Delta\|_F}{\alpha(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})} . \end{equation} If $\varepsilon<1-\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$, then \begin{align} \|\widetilde C-C^{*}\|_F &\le \frac{\kappa(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})}{\sqrt{1-4\varepsilon+2\varepsilon^{2}}}\,\|\Delta\|_F,\\ \|\widetilde B-B^{*}\|_2 &\le \frac{\|B^{*}\|_2^{2}}{1-\|B^{*}\|_2\|\Delta\|_F}\,\|\Delta\|_F. \end{align}
assumptions: Let $A\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$ with decomposition $(B^{*},C^{*})$ given by Theorem~\ref{thm:general_decomposition} for a nonzero subspace ${\mathcal{S}}$, and let $\widetilde A=A+\Delta\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$ have decomposition $(\widetilde B,\widetilde C)$ for the same ${\mathcal{S}}$.
conclusions: \|\widetilde C-C^{*}\|_F &\le \frac{\kappa(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})}{\sqrt{1-4\varepsilon+2\varepsilon^{2}}}\,\|\Delta\|_F,
nodes.statement_short: For a perturbation with $\varepsilon=\|B^*\|_2^3\|\Delta\|_F/\alpha(B^*,{\mathcal{S}})<1-1/\sqrt2$, $C^*$ moves by $O(\kappa\|\Delta\|_F)$ and $B^*$ by $O(\|B^*\|_2^2\|\Delta\|_F)$.
nodes.label: prop:perturbation_fro

nodes.name: Smallness parameter $\varepsilon$
nodes.statement: \varepsilon:=\|B^{*}\|_2\,\kappa(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})^{2}\,\|\Delta\|_F =\frac{\|B^{*}\|_2^{3}\,\|\Delta\|_F}{\alpha(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})} .
nodes.label: eq:smallness_fro

nodes.name: Stability bound for $C^*$
nodes.statement: \|\widetilde C-C^{*}\|_F &\le \frac{\kappa(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})}{\sqrt{1-4\varepsilon+2\varepsilon^{2}}}\,\|\Delta\|_F,
nodes.label: eq:C_stab_fro

nodes.name: Interpretation of the stability bounds
nodes.statement: The bound~\eqref{eq:B_stab_fro} is free of $\alpha(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})$, whereas~\eqref{eq:C_stab_fro} degrades with the restricted condition number $\kappa(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})$ of~\eqref{eq:kappa_def}. Both inflation factors decrease to $1$ as $\|\Delta\|_F\to0$, recovering the infinitesimal rates $\kappa(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})$ and $\|B^{*}\|_2^{2}$ of~\eqref{eq:dC_bound} and~\eqref{eq:dB_bound}. Along any sequence with $\alpha(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})\to0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha_lipschitz}\textbf{(i)} gives $\lambda_{\min}(B^{*})\to0$, hence $\lambda_{\max}(A-C^{*})=\lambda_{\max}\big((B^{*})^{-1}\big)\to\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: The $B$-bound is free of $\alpha$; the $C$-bound degrades with $\kappa$; both recover the infinitesimal rates as $\Delta\to0$.

nodes.name: Uniform stability on compact sets
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathcal{S}}$ be nonzero and let $\Theta\subset\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$ be nonempty, compact and convex, and set \[ \beta_0:=\max_{A\in\Theta}\|B^{*}(A)\|_2, \qquad \alpha_0:=\min_{A\in\Theta}\alpha\big(B^{*}(A),{\mathcal{S}}\big). \] Then, for all $A,\widetilde A\in\Theta$, \[ \|C^{*}(\widetilde A)-C^{*}(A)\|_F\le\frac{\beta_0}{\sqrt{\alpha_0}}\,\|\widetilde A-A\|_F, \qquad \|B^{*}(\widetilde A)-B^{*}(A)\|_2\le \beta_0^{2}\,\|\widetilde A-A\|_F . \]
assumptions: Let ${\mathcal{S}}$ be nonzero and let $\Theta\subset\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$ be nonempty, compact and convex,
conclusions: \|C^{*}(\widetilde A)-C^{*}(A)\|_F\le\frac{\beta_0}{\sqrt{\alpha_0}}\,\|\widetilde A-A\|_F,
\|B^{*}(\widetilde A)-B^{*}(A)\|_2\le \beta_0^{2}\,\|\widetilde A-A\|_F .
nodes.statement_short: On a compact convex $\Theta$, $C^*$ and $B^*$ are Lipschitz with constants $\beta_0/\sqrt{\alpha_0}$ and $\beta_0^2$.
nodes.label: cor:perturbation_global

nodes.name: Primal convex program for the decomposition
nodes.statement: Writing $C(x)=\sum_{k=1}^m x_k D_k$ and $\Phi(x):=-\log\det\bigl(A-C(x)\bigr)$, the decomposition is obtained by solving the convex optimization problem \begin{equation} x^\ast \;\in\; arg\,min_{x\in\Omega_x}\;\Phi(x), \end{equation} and then setting $C^\ast=C(x^\ast)$ and $B^\ast=M(x^\ast)^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize $\Phi(x)=-\log\det(A-C(x))$ over $\Omega_x$; then $C^*=C(x^*)$, $B^*=M(x^*)^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Primal problem in coordinates $x$
nodes.statement: x^\ast \;\in\; arg\,min_{x\in\Omega_x}\;\Phi(x),

nodes.name: Hessian of $\Phi$
nodes.statement: Differentiating once more yields the Hessian \begin{equation} \frac{\partial^2\Phi}{\partial x_k\partial x_\ell}(x) = \mathrm{tr}\big(B(x)D_kB(x)D_\ell\big), \qquad k,\ell=1,\dots,m. \end{equation}
conclusions: \frac{\partial^2\Phi}{\partial x_k\partial x_\ell}(x) = \mathrm{tr}\big(B(x)D_kB(x)D_\ell\big),

nodes.name: Hessian formula
nodes.statement: \frac{\partial^2\Phi}{\partial x_k\partial x_\ell}(x) = \mathrm{tr}\big(B(x)D_kB(x)D_\ell\big), \qquad k,\ell=1,\dots,m.
nodes.label: eq:hess_section2

nodes.name: Positive definiteness of the Hessian; strict convexity of $\Phi$
nodes.statement:
Writing $D(v):=\sum_{\ell=1}^m v_\ell D_\ell$ for $v\in\mathbb{R}^m$, the Hessian $H(x):=

eq0$, since the basis matrices $D_k$ are linearly independent and hence $D(v)
eq0$. Thus $H(x)\succ0$ for all $x\in\Omega_x$, and $\Phi$ is strictly convex on $\Omega_x$.
conclusions: Thus $H(x)\succ0$ for all $x\in\Omega_x$, and $\Phi$ is strictly convex on $\Omega_x$.
nodes.statement_short: $v^\top H(x)v=\|B^{1/2}D(v)B^{1/2}\|_F^2>0$ for $v\ne0$, so $\Phi$ is strictly convex.

nodes.name: Analytic derivatives via linear solves with $M(x)$
nodes.statement: All derivatives of $\Phi$ are computed using explicit analytic expressions and require only applications of $M(x)^{-1}$, implemented through a factorization or structure-exploiting solver for $M(x)$. No numerical differentiation is used. In the structured settings the inverse $B(x)$ is never formed, since only the entries of $M(x)^{-1}$ on the supports of the $D_k$ are needed. In the dense case it is formed once per outer iteration, as accounted for in Section~\ref{subsec:complexity_brief}. If $B^\ast$ is required explicitly it is formed once on exit, at cost $O(n^3)$.
nodes.statement_short: Derivatives need only solves with $M(x)$; in structured cases only entries of $M^{-1}$ on the supports of the $D_k$.

nodes.name: Hessian-vector product formula
nodes.statement: The Newton-CG method requires only Hessian-vector products. With $D(v)$ as above, \begin{equation} \big(H(x)v\big)_k = \mathrm{tr}\big(B(x)D_kB(x)D(v)\big), \qquad k=1,\dots,m, \end{equation} which can be evaluated using the same linear solves with $M(x)$.
conclusions: \big(H(x)v\big)_k = \mathrm{tr}\big(B(x)D_kB(x)D(v)\big),

nodes.name: Hessian-vector product
nodes.statement: \big(H(x)v\big)_k = \mathrm{tr}\big(B(x)D_kB(x)D(v)\big), \qquad k=1,\dots,m,

nodes.name: Argument for global convergence of Newton-CG
nodes.statement: The objective $\Phi(x)=-\log\det\bigl(A-C(x)\bigr)$ is strictly convex and self-concordant on $\Omega_x$, as it is the composition of the self-concordant log-determinant barrier with an affine map. By Theorem~\ref{thm:general_decomposition} and Lemma~\ref{lem:bounded_intersection}, the sublevel set $\{x:\Phi(x)\le\Phi(x_0)\}$ of any feasible $x_0$ is nonempty, compact, and bounded away from $\partial\Omega_x$.
nodes.statement_short: Self-concordance of the log-det barrier composed with an affine map, plus compact sublevel sets from the theorem and lemma.

nodes.name: Global convergence of feasibility-preserving Newton-CG
nodes.statement: Consequently, Newton-CG with feasibility-preserving Armijo backtracking is globally convergent from any feasible initialization, provided each CG solve is terminated by an inexact-Newton forcing condition \begin{equation} \|H(x_k)d_k+g(x_k)\|_2\le\eta_k\,\|g(x_k)\|_2, \qquad \eta_k\le\bar\eta<1 . \end{equation}
assumptions: provided each CG solve is terminated by an inexact-Newton forcing condition \begin{equation} \|H(x_k)d_k+g(x_k)\|_2\le\eta_k\,\|g(x_k)\|_2, \qquad \eta_k\le\bar\eta<1 . \end{equation}
conclusions: Newton-CG with feasibility-preserving Armijo backtracking is globally convergent from any feasible initialization,

nodes.name: Inexact-Newton forcing condition
nodes.statement: \|H(x_k)d_k+g(x_k)\|_2\le\eta_k\,\|g(x_k)\|_2, \qquad \eta_k\le\bar\eta<1 .
nodes.label: eq:forcing

nodes.name: CG iterates are descent directions
nodes.statement: Started from $d=0$, every CG iterate is a descent direction, since $H(x_k)\succ0$.
conclusions: every CG iterate is a descent direction,

nodes.name: Local convergence rates under the forcing sequence
nodes.statement: The \emph{local} rate is governed by the forcing sequence $\{\eta_k\}$ rather than by a fixed tolerance: $\eta_k\le\bar\eta<1$ gives a linear rate, $\eta_k\to0$ a superlinear one, and $\eta_k=O(\|g(x_k)\|_2)$ a quadratic one, in which case full Newton steps are eventually accepted near the unique minimizer $x^\ast$. See, e.g., \cite{dembo1982inexact,nesterov1994interior,nocedal2006numerical}.
conclusions: $\eta_k\le\bar\eta<1$ gives a linear rate, $\eta_k\to0$ a superlinear one, and $\eta_k=O(\|g(x_k)\|_2)$ a quadratic one,
nodes.statement_short: Linear, superlinear or quadratic local rate according to the forcing sequence (standard inexact-Newton theory).

nodes.name: Per-iteration cost of dense Newton-CG
nodes.statement: The dense bounds assume unstructured basis matrices $D_k$, so each trace evaluation costs $O(n^2)$. Each conjugate-gradient step forms a Hessian--vector product $H(x)p$ via~\eqref{eq:Hv_formula}, which requires applying $M(x)^{-1}$ to the dense combination $D(p)=\sum_\ell p_\ell D_\ell$. In the dense case this is a $O(n^3)$ solve (with $M(x)$ factored once per outer iteration), in addition to $O(mn^2)$ for the $m$ trace evaluations; hence a Newton-CG outer iteration costs $O\big(n^3+N_{\mathrm{cg}}(n^3+mn^2)\big)$. Precomputing the $m$ matrices $M(x)^{-1}D_k$ instead costs $O(mn^3)$ once, with $O(mn^2)$ storage, and reduces each CG step to $O(mn^2)$. This pays only when the number of CG steps is large relative to $m$. The structured rows of Table~\ref{tab:per_iteration_complexity} follow the same accounting, with the dense solve cost $n^3$ replaced by the corresponding structured solve cost.
nodes.statement_short: Dense Newton-CG costs $O(n^3+N_{cg}(n^3+mn^2))$ per outer iteration; precomputing $M^{-1}D_k$ pays only for many CG steps.

nodes.name: Banded setting: structure-preserving solves and traces
nodes.statement: In the banded setting, both $A$ and the constraint subspace ${\mathcal{S}}$ are chosen so that $M(x)$ remains banded along the optimization path, with half-bandwidth $b$, meaning that entries vanish for $|i-j|>b$. Linear solves and trace evaluations are then carried out in $O(nb^2)$ and $O(b^2)$ time, respectively. Although $M(x)^{-1}$ is dense in general, the trace terms involve only entries of $M(x)^{-1}$ within the sparsity pattern of the banded matrices $D_k$, which can be computed efficiently using sparse inverse subset methods (e.g., Takahashi-type recursions, see \cite{rue2005gaussian}). In the banded row, the term $mb^2$ bounds the $m$ trace evaluations when each $D_k$ is supported on a $b\times b$ block. For the standard banded basis, in which each $D_k$ has $O(1)$ nonzero entries, this term reduces to $O(m)$.
nodes.statement_short: If $M(x)$ stays banded, solves cost $O(nb^2)$ and traces $O(b^2)$ via sparse-inverse (Takahashi) recursions.

nodes.name: Banded Hessian-vector products
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eq:Hv_formula}, a conjugate-gradient step requires \begin{align*} \big(H(x)v\big)_k &=\mathrm{tr}\big(M(x)^{-1}D_k\,M(x)^{-1}D(v)\big) =\big\langle D_k,\,G\big\rangle_F,\\ G&:=M(x)^{-1}D(v)\,M(x)^{-1}, \end{align*} so only the entries of $G$ on the supports of the $D_k$ are needed, that is, the band of $G$. Unlike the gradient traces, this does not reduce to a single structured solve: the matrix $M(x)^{-1}$ is dense and occurs \emph{twice} in $G$, so applying it successively to $D(v)$ produces a dense intermediate and costs $O(n^2)$ or more per product. The band of $G$ is nevertheless computable in $O(nb^2)$. Indeed, \begin{equation} G=-\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\big(M(x)+t\,D(v)\big)^{-1}, \end{equation} so the required entries of $G$ form the directional derivative of the selected inverse of $M(x)$. Equivalently, $G$ is the off-diagonal block of the inverse of the $2n\times2n$ matrix \[ \begin{pmatrix} M(x) & -D(v)\\ 0 & M(x)\end{pmatrix}, \] which is banded once the two copies are interleaved, index $i$ of the first placed next to index $i$ of the second. In the ordering displayed above the off-diagonal block instead sits $n$ positions away from the diagonal. Grouping the indices into $n/b$ consecutive blocks of size $b$ makes $M(x)$ block tridiagonal. The block $LDL^\top$ factorization and the block Takahashi recursion then each consist of $n/b$ steps of $O(b^3)$ work, and propagating forward-mode derivatives through both recursions costs the same. The band of $G$ obtained this way is exact. This is a manifestation of the quasiseparable structure of the inverse of a banded matrix \cite{vandebril2008matrix,erisman1975computing}: the mechanism that makes the gradient traces cheap also makes the second-order terms cheap, and it is what the $nb^2$ entries of Table~\ref{tab:per_iteration_complexity} rest on.
nodes.statement_short: The band of $G=M^{-1}D(v)M^{-1}$ is a directional derivative of the selected inverse and is computable in $O(nb^2)$ by differentiating the block Takahashi recursion.
nodes.label: rem:banded_hessvec

nodes.name: $G$ as a derivative of the inverse
nodes.statement: G=-\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\big(M(x)+t\,D(v)\big)^{-1},
nodes.label: eq:G_as_derivative

nodes.name: Circulant setting: FFT diagonalization
nodes.statement: In the circulant setting, $A$ and the basis matrices $\{D_k\}$ are circulant and symmetric, so that $M(x)$ remains circulant along the optimization path and is diagonalized by the discrete Fourier transform: writing $F$ for the unitary discrete Fourier matrix, a symmetric circulant matrix has the form $F^{-1}\mathrm{diag}(\cdot)F$, the diagonal holding its eigenvalues. Let $\mu,\delta,d_k\in\mathbb{R}^n$ be the eigenvalue vectors of $M(x)$, $D(v)$ and $D_k$, so that $M(x)=F^{-1}\mathrm{diag}(\mu)F$, $D(v)=F^{-1}\mathrm{diag}(\delta)F$ and $D_k=F^{-1}\mathrm{diag}(d_k)F$. The two-sided product is then again circulant, and \eqref{eq:Hv_formula} becomes a pointwise product of these vectors, \begin{align} M(x)^{-1}D(v)M(x)^{-1}&=F^{-1}\mathrm{diag}(\delta/\mu^{2})F ,\nonumber\\ \big(H(x)v\big)_k&=\sum_{j}(d_k)_j\,\delta_j/\mu_j^{2} . \end{align} Two fast Fourier transforms produce $\mu$ and $\delta$ in $O(n\log n)$, after which all $m$ trace evaluations amount to a single $m\times n$ matrix--vector product. This is the one structured case in which the second-order terms are exactly diagonalized. See, e.g., \cite{gray2006toeplitz,gohberg1994fast}.
nodes.statement_short: Circulant $M(x)$ is diagonalized by the DFT, so Hessian-vector products are pointwise products after two FFTs.

nodes.name: Circulant Hessian-vector product
nodes.statement: M(x)^{-1}D(v)M(x)^{-1}&=F^{-1}\mathrm{diag}(\delta/\mu^{2})F ,\nonumber\\ \big(H(x)v\big)_k&=\sum_{j}(d_k)_j\,\delta_j/\mu_j^{2} .
nodes.label: eq:circulant_G

nodes.name: General Toeplitz setting
nodes.statement: For a general Toeplitz $M(x)$, linear solves remain fast, requiring $O(n^2)$ time by Levinson/Schur-type recursions. The second-order terms, however, lose the structure, since the inverse of a Toeplitz matrix is again Toeplitz only in special cases, so at this generality $M(x)^{-1}D(v)M(x)^{-1}$ retains the dense bound.

nodes.name: Basis $\{E_k\}$ of ${\mathcal{S}}^\perp$ and dual dimension $m^\perp$
nodes.statement: Let $\{E_1,\dots,E_{m^\perp}\}$ be a basis of ${\mathcal{S}}^\perp$, where \begin{equation} m^\perp := \dim({\mathcal{S}}^\perp)=\tfrac{n(n+1)}2-m. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Dual dimension $m^\perp$
nodes.statement: m^\perp := \dim({\mathcal{S}}^\perp)=\tfrac{n(n+1)}2-m.

nodes.name: Dual parametrization $B(y)$
nodes.statement: Fix any $B_0\in {\mathcal{S}}^\perp\cap\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$ and write \begin{equation} B(y) := B_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{m^\perp} y_k E_k, \qquad y\in\mathbb{R}^{m^\perp}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Dual parametrization
nodes.statement: B(y) := B_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{m^\perp} y_k E_k, \qquad y\in\mathbb{R}^{m^\perp}.

nodes.name: Feasible initialization of the dual
nodes.statement: Unlike the primal formulation, which is always initialized at $x=0$ (feasible since $A\succ0$), the dual requires such a feasible $B_0$. Obtaining one is, in general, a feasibility (phase-one) step: a semidefinite program in the same $m^\perp$ variables as~\eqref{eq:dual_problem_section2}, whose solvability is guaranteed by Theorem~\ref{thm:general_decomposition}. In the structured cases of interest this step is immediate: whenever every matrix in ${\mathcal{S}}$ has zero diagonal, as for zero-diagonal and off-diagonal prescribed-support constraints, $\mathrm{tr}(I_nX)=\mathrm{tr}(X)=0$ for all $X\in {\mathcal{S}}$, so $I_n\in {\mathcal{S}}^\perp$ and one may take $B_0=I_n$, with analogous explicit choices in the banded and group-invariant settings.
nodes.statement_short: The dual needs a feasible $B_0$ (a phase-one SDP in general); $B_0=I_n$ works when ${\mathcal{S}}$ has zero diagonal.

nodes.name: Dual objective $\Psi(y)$
nodes.statement: Define \begin{equation} \Psi(y) := \log\det\bigl(B(y)\bigr)-\mathrm{tr}\bigl(AB(y)\bigr)+n. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Dual objective in coordinates
nodes.statement: \Psi(y) := \log\det\bigl(B(y)\bigr)-\mathrm{tr}\bigl(AB(y)\bigr)+n.

nodes.name: Gradient and Hessian of the dual objective
nodes.statement: Then \begin{align} \frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial y_k}(y) &= \mathrm{tr}\big(B(y)^{-1}E_k\big)-\mathrm{tr}(AE_k), \nonumber \\ \frac{\partial^2\Psi}{\partial y_k\partial y_\ell}(y) &= -\mathrm{tr}\big(B(y)^{-1}E_kB(y)^{-1}E_\ell\big), \qquad k,\ell=1,\dots,m^\perp . \end{align}
conclusions: \frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial y_k}(y) &= \mathrm{tr}\big(B(y)^{-1}E_k\big)-\mathrm{tr}(AE_k), \nonumber \\ \frac{\partial^2\Psi}{\partial y_k\partial y_\ell}(y) &= -\mathrm{tr}\big(B(y)^{-1}E_kB(y)^{-1}E_\ell\big), \qquad k,\ell=1,\dots,m^\perp .

nodes.name: Dual gradient and Hessian
nodes.statement: \frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial y_k}(y) &= \mathrm{tr}\big(B(y)^{-1}E_k\big)-\mathrm{tr}(AE_k), \nonumber \\ \frac{\partial^2\Psi}{\partial y_k\partial y_\ell}(y) &= -\mathrm{tr}\big(B(y)^{-1}E_kB(y)^{-1}E_\ell\big), \qquad k,\ell=1,\dots,m^\perp .

nodes.name: Finite symmetry group with $A$ and ${\mathcal{S}}$ invariant
nodes.statement: Assume that a finite group $\mathcal G\subset{\mathcal{O}}(n)$ acts on $\mathbb{S}^n$ by conjugation $X\mapsto P X P^\top$, and that both $A$ and ${\mathcal{S}}$ are $\mathcal G$-invariant.

nodes.name: Fixed-point subspace ${\mathcal{S}}^{\mathcal G}$ and $m_{\mathcal G}$
nodes.statement: Define \begin{equation} {\mathcal{S}}^{\mathcal G} := \{X\in {\mathcal{S}}:\;P X P^\top=X\ \forall P\in\mathcal G\}, \qquad m_{\mathcal G} := \dim {\mathcal{S}}^{\mathcal G} \le m. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Fixed-point subspace
nodes.statement: {\mathcal{S}}^{\mathcal G} := \{X\in {\mathcal{S}}:\;P X P^\top=X\ \forall P\in\mathcal G\}, \qquad m_{\mathcal G} := \dim {\mathcal{S}}^{\mathcal G} \le m.

nodes.name: Reduction of the optimization to the fixed-point subspace
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eq:G_fixed}, the unique minimizer $C^\ast$ lies in ${\mathcal{S}}^{\mathcal G}$. Writing \begin{equation} C(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{m_{\mathcal G}} x_k \widetilde D_k, \end{equation} where $\{\widetilde D_k\}$ is a basis of ${\mathcal{S}}^{\mathcal G}$, the optimization problem reduces to dimension $m_{\mathcal G}$. Newton-CG applies verbatim with the reduced derivatives.
conclusions: the unique minimizer $C^\ast$ lies in ${\mathcal{S}}^{\mathcal G}$.
the optimization problem reduces to dimension $m_{\mathcal G}$.

nodes.name: Reduced parametrization
nodes.statement: C(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{m_{\mathcal G}} x_k \widetilde D_k,

nodes.name: Per-iteration cost of group-invariant Newton-CG
nodes.statement: The per-iteration cost is that of Table~\ref{tab:per_iteration_complexity} with $m$ replaced by $m_{\mathcal G}$. In the generic dense case, \begin{equation} T_{\mathrm{Newton}}^{\mathcal G} = O\big(n^3+N_{\mathrm{cg}}(n^3+m_{\mathcal G} n^2)\big). \end{equation} Reducing the optimization dimension from $m$ to $m_{\mathcal G}$ shrinks the number of trace evaluations, but not the $n\times n$ linear algebra: $M(x)$ is still an $n\times n$ matrix that must be factorized once per outer iteration, and each Hessian--vector product still applies $M(x)^{-1}$ twice. To this one adds the cost $T_{\mathrm{fact}}(\mathcal G)$ of the symmetry-adapted change of basis. That transform depends only on $\mathcal G$ and not on the iterate, so it is computed once before the iteration begins, outside the per-iteration cost.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetry reduces the number of traces to $m_{\mathcal G}$ but not the $n\times n$ linear algebra; the change of basis is a one-time cost.

nodes.name: Group-invariant dense cost
nodes.statement: T_{\mathrm{Newton}}^{\mathcal G} = O\big(n^3+N_{\mathrm{cg}}(n^3+m_{\mathcal G} n^2)\big).
nodes.label: eq:group_newton_cost

nodes.name: Block-permutation symmetry: cost independent of $n$
nodes.statement: Further reduction occurs when the symmetry shrinks $M(x)$ itself. In the block-permutation setting of the last row of Table~\ref{tab:per_iteration_complexity}, Example~IV of Appendix~\ref{app:examples}, $\mathcal G$ permutes $r$ blocks and every $\mathcal G$-invariant matrix is determined by $O(r^2)$ coefficients, one for each off-diagonal block pair and two for each diagonal block. The symmetry-adapted transform is a block averaging, so $T_{\mathrm{fact}}(\mathcal G)$ is one $O(n^2)$ pass over $A$, and nothing when $A$ is supplied by its block coefficients. Solves with $M(x)$ and the two-sided products of Remark~\ref{rem:banded_hessvec} then act on $r\times r$ data at cost $O(r^3)$, and each of the $m_{\mathcal G}$ trace evaluations costs $O(r^2)$, giving a per-iteration complexity independent of $n$: \begin{equation} T_{\mathrm{Newton}}^{\mathcal G,\,r\text{ blocks}} = O\big(r^3+N_{\mathrm{cg}}(r^3+m_{\mathcal G} r^2)\big), \qquad m_{\mathcal G}\le r(r+1)/2 . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: When $\mathcal G$ acts by blocks, every invariant matrix has $O(r^2)$ coefficients and an iteration costs $O(r^3+N_{cg}(r^3+m_{\mathcal G}r^2))$.

nodes.name: Block-permutation cost
nodes.statement: T_{\mathrm{Newton}}^{\mathcal G,\,r\text{ blocks}} = O\big(r^3+N_{\mathrm{cg}}(r^3+m_{\mathcal G} r^2)\big), \qquad m_{\mathcal G}\le r(r+1)/2 .
nodes.label: eq:group_block_cost

nodes.name: Cost of the symmetry-adapted transform
nodes.statement: For general finite groups, $T_{\mathrm{fact}}(\mathcal G)$ may be comparable to dense linear algebra. For certain groups, special algebraic structure yields fast transforms (e.g. FFTs for cyclic groups), dramatically reducing $T_{\mathrm{fact}}(\mathcal G)$.

nodes.name: Time horizon $N$
nodes.statement: Let \(N\in\mathbb{N}\) denote the time horizon.

nodes.name: Tradable assets and their increments $X^i_j$
nodes.statement: At each time \(i=1,\dots,N\), suppose that \(p_i\in\mathbb{N}\) risky assets are available for trading, with increments $ X^i_1,\dots,X^i_{p_i}. $

nodes.name: Non-tradable risk factors $X^i_{p_i+1},\dots,X^i_{q_i}$
nodes.statement: In addition, we allow for further random variables $ X^i_{p_i+1},\dots,X^i_{q_i}$, $q_i\ge p_i,$ which represent increments of other risky factors or assets that may influence the market but are not tradable at time \(i\).

nodes.name: Information vector $Y^i$
nodes.statement: The information available for trading at time \(i\) is generated by the random vector \[ Y^i=(Y^i_1,\dots,Y^i_{m_i}) = \bigl( X^1_1,\dots,X^1_{q_1},\; \dots,\; X^{i-1}_1,\dots,X^{i-1}_{q_{i-1}} \bigr) A^i, \] where \(m_i \le \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} q_j\) and \(A^i\) is a deterministic matrix.
nodes.statement_short: The information at time $i$ is a fixed linear transform $Y^i$ of all past increments.

nodes.name: Gaussian increments $Z\sim\mathcal N(0,\Sigma)$
nodes.statement: Let \(n=\sum_{i=1}^N q_i\), and assume that the random vector \[ Z=(Z_1,...,Z_n):=\bigl(X^1_1,\dots,X^1_{q_1},\;\dots,\;X^N_1,\dots,X^N_{q_N}\bigr) \] has a non-degenerate multivariate normal distribution with mean zero (for simplicity) and covariance matrix \(\Sigma\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}\).

nodes.name: Precision matrix $\Lambda$
nodes.statement: Denote by \({\Lambda}=\Sigma^{-1}\) the corresponding precision matrix.

nodes.name: Trading strategy $\gamma$
nodes.statement: A trading strategy is a random vector $ \gamma=\bigl( \gamma^1_1,\dots,\gamma^1_{p_1},\; \dots,\; \gamma^N_1,\dots,\gamma^N_{p_N} \bigr), $ where \(\gamma^i_j\) denotes the number of shares held in the risky asset with increment \(X^i_j\).

nodes.name: Measurability of positions
nodes.statement: The position \(\gamma^i_j\) is required to be \(Y^i\)-measurable, that is, \begin{equation} \gamma^i_j = g^i_j(Y^i) \; \text{for a measurable}\ g^i_j:\mathbb{R}^{m_i}\to\mathbb{R}, \, i=1,\dots,N,\ j=1,\dots,p_i. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Positions as measurable functions of $Y^i$
nodes.statement: \gamma^i_j = g^i_j(Y^i) \; \text{for a measurable}\ g^i_j:\mathbb{R}^{m_i}\to\mathbb{R}, \, i=1,\dots,N,\ j=1,\dots,p_i.
nodes.label: strategy

nodes.name: Terminal portfolio value $V^\gamma$
nodes.statement: The corresponding terminal portfolio value is \begin{equation} V^\gamma = \sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^{p_i}\gamma^i_jX^i_j. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Terminal portfolio value
nodes.statement: V^\gamma = \sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^{p_i}\gamma^i_jX^i_j.
nodes.label: portfolio

nodes.name: Admissible strategies $\mathcal A$
nodes.statement: We denote by \(\mathcal A\) the set of all trading strategies \(\gamma\) for which \(V^\gamma\) is integrable under every centered nondegenerate Gaussian law of \(Z\), which is what makes the change-of-measure identities used below well defined.

nodes.name: Linear strategies $\mathcal A_l$
nodes.statement: Let \(\mathcal A_l \subset \mathcal A\) be the set of trading strategies corresponding to linear functions $g^i_j$ in~\eqref{strategy} ($g^i_j(0)=0$).

nodes.name: Linear strategies give quadratic, integrable terminal values
nodes.statement: For these $V^\gamma$ is a quadratic form in $Z$ and the integrability requirement holds automatically.
conclusions: $V^\gamma$ is a quadratic form in $Z$ and the integrability requirement holds automatically.

nodes.name: Representing matrices $D^{i,j,k}$
nodes.statement: For any \(i=1,\ldots,N\), \(j=1,\ldots,p_i\), and \(k=1,\ldots,m_i\), the product \(Y^i_k X^i_j\) can be represented as, \begin{equation} Y^i_k X^i_j = -\frac{1}{2}\, Z D^{i,j,k} Z^\top, \end{equation} where \(D^{i,j,k}\in\mathbb{S}^n\) is the unique symmetric matrix representing this quadratic form.

nodes.name: Quadratic-form representation of $Y^i_kX^i_j$
nodes.statement: Y^i_k X^i_j = -\frac{1}{2}\, Z D^{i,j,k} Z^\top,
nodes.label: representation

nodes.name: The matrices $D^{i,j,k}$ have zero diagonal
nodes.statement: Since the random vector $Y^i$ is determined by $X^r_j$, $r<i$, $j=1,\ldots,q_r$, we obtain that $D^{i,j,k}$ is a zero-diagonal matrix.
assumptions: Since the random vector $Y^i$ is determined by $X^r_j$, $r<i$, $j=1,\ldots,q_r$,
conclusions: $D^{i,j,k}$ is a zero-diagonal matrix.

nodes.name: Strategy subspace ${\mathcal{D}}$
nodes.statement: Let \({\mathcal{D}}\subset\mathbb{S}^n\) denote the linear span of all matrices of the form \(D^{i,j,k}\).

nodes.name: Linear strategies correspond to matrices in ${\mathcal{D}}$
nodes.statement: A strategy \(\gamma\) lies in \(\mathcal A_l\) if and only if there exists $X\in{\mathcal{D}}$ such that \begin{equation} V^{\gamma} = -\frac{1}{2} Z X Z^\top . \end{equation}
conclusions: A strategy \(\gamma\) lies in \(\mathcal A_l\) if and only if there exists $X\in{\mathcal{D}}$ such that \begin{equation} V^{\gamma} = -\frac{1}{2} Z X Z^\top . \end{equation}

nodes.name: Linear strategy as a quadratic form
nodes.statement: V^{\gamma} = -\frac{1}{2} Z X Z^\top .
nodes.label: eq:v_gamma_bilinear

nodes.name: Exponential utility
nodes.statement: The investor’s preferences are described by the exponential utility function \[ u(x)=-\exp(-\rho x), \qquad x\in\mathbb{R}, \] with absolute risk aversion parameter \(\rho>0\).

nodes.name: Exponential utility maximization
nodes.statement: The optimization problem is therefore \begin{equation} \max_{\gamma\in\mathcal{A}} \ \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[-\exp\!\left(-\rho V^\gamma\right)\right], \end{equation} where \(\mathbb{P}\) is the probability measure under which the Gaussian vectors \(X^i_j\) and \(Y^i\) introduced above are distributed, and \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}\) denotes expectation with respect to it.
nodes.statement_short: Maximize $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}[-\exp(-\rho V^\gamma)]$ over admissible strategies.

nodes.name: Exponential utility maximization problem
nodes.statement: \max_{\gamma\in\mathcal{A}} \ \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}\!\left[-\exp\!\left(-\rho V^\gamma\right)\right],
nodes.label: eq:exp_util

nodes.name: Normalization of risk aversion to $\rho=1$
nodes.statement: For any $\gamma\in\mathcal A$ and \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\) we have $\lambda\gamma\in\mathcal A$ and \(V^{\lambda\gamma}=\lambda V^\gamma\). Hence, without loss of generality, we set \(\rho:=1\).

nodes.name: Utility maximization as a log-det problem over ${\mathcal{D}}$
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eq:v_gamma_bilinear}, a linear trading strategy corresponds to a matrix \(X\in{\mathcal{D}}\) with terminal value \(-\frac12 ZXZ^\top\), so that \({\mathcal{D}}\) is the matrix counterpart of the set of admissible linear strategies. nodes.name: Scope of the Gaussian exponential-utility framework
nodes.statement: The framework of Proposition \ref{thm:finance_value} shows that, in the Gaussian setting with exponential utility, the optimal portfolio is linear and can be characterized through a specific matrix decomposition. The model accommodates partial information, non-traded assets, the trading of indices rather than individual securities, and an information structure that need not be a filtration, so that information may be lost over time.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition (exponential utility)
nodes.statement: Every matrix in \({\mathcal{D}}\) has zero diagonal. If \(X\in{\mathcal{D}}\cap\mathbb S_+^n\), then \(X\) is positive semidefinite and \(X_{ii}=0\) for every \(i\). For a positive semidefinite matrix, $ |X_{ij}|^2\le X_{ii}X_{jj}=0$, and therefore \(X_{ij}=0\) for every \(i,j\). Hence \(X=0\), and consequently $ {\mathcal{D}}\cap\mathbb S_+^n=\{0\}. $ Thus, condition~\eqref{eq:nopsddirections} holds, and Theorem~\ref{thm:general_decomposition} yields the existence and uniqueness of the decomposition~\eqref{eq:finance_decomposition}. Define a probability measure $\hat{\mathbb Q}$ such that the distribution of $(Z_1,...,Z_n)$ is multivariate normal with mean zero and covariance matrix $\hat Q$. From \eqref{representation} it follows that for any \(i=1,\ldots,N\), \(j=1,\ldots,p_i\), and \(k=1,\ldots,m_i\) \[ \mathbb E_{\hat{\mathbb Q}}\left[Y^i_k X^i_j\right] = -\frac{1}{2}\mathbb E_{\hat{\mathbb Q}}\left[Z D^{i,j,k} Z^\top\right]=-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}\left(D^{i,j,k} \hat Q\right)=0. \] Hence, since $Z$ is Gaussian and the above cross-covariances vanish, the random vectors $(X^i_1,\dots,X^i_{p_i})$ and $Y^i$ are independent under $\hat{\mathbb Q}$ for any $i\leq N$. Thus, from the tower property of conditional expectation we conclude \begin{equation} \mathbb E_{\hat{\mathbb Q}}\left[V^{\gamma}\right]=0, \ \ \forall \gamma\in\mathcal A. \end{equation} Next, choose $\gamma\in\mathcal A$. For any $z>0$ \begin{align*} \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \gamma}\right)\right] &=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \gamma}\right)+z \frac{d{\hat{\mathbb Q}}}{d\mathbb P}V^{\gamma}\right]\\ &\geq \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[z\frac{d{\hat{\mathbb Q}}}{d\mathbb P}\left(1-\log \left(z\frac{d{\hat{\mathbb Q}}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right)\right]\\ &=z-z\log z-z\mathbb E_{\hat{\mathbb Q}}\left[\log \left(\frac{d{\hat{\mathbb Q}}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]. \end{align*} The first equality is due to \eqref{nuetral}. The above inequality follows from the well-known relation $xy \leq e^x+y(\log y-1)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}, y>0$ by setting $x=-V^{\gamma}$ and $y=z\frac{d\hat{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}$, and rearranging terms. The last equality is straightforward. From simple calculus it follows that the concave function defined for $z>0$ by $$z\mapsto z-z\log z-z\,\mathbb E_{\hat{\mathbb Q}}\left[\log \left(\frac{d{\hat{\mathbb Q}}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]$$ attains its maximum at $z^{*}:=\exp\left(-\mathbb E_{\hat{\mathbb Q}}\left[\log \left(\frac{d{\hat{\mathbb Q}}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]\right)$ and the corresponding maximal value is also $z^{*}$. Thus, \begin{equation} \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{ \gamma}\right)\right]\geq \exp\left(-\mathbb E_{\hat{\mathbb Q}}\left[\log \left(\frac{d{\hat{\mathbb Q}}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]\right), \ \ \forall \gamma\in\mathcal A. \end{equation} The bound \eqref{lowerbound} was derived for an arbitrary $\gamma\in\mathcal A$, with no restriction to $\mathcal A_l$. We now exhibit a \emph{candidate} strategy attaining it. Since $\hat\Gamma\in{\mathcal{D}}$, the characterization \eqref{eq:v_gamma_bilinear} supplies a strategy $\hat\gamma\in\mathcal A_l$ satisfying \eqref{eq:optimal_v_gamma_bilinear}. At this stage $\hat\gamma$ is only a candidate, and its optimality is established below. For multivariate normal distributions the likelihood ratio is \begin{equation} \frac{d{{\hat{\mathbb Q}}}}{d\mathbb P}=\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}Z\hat Q^{-1}Z^\top \right)/\det(\hat Q)^{1/2}}{\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}Z {\Lambda} Z^\top\right)/\det(\Sigma)^{1/2}}. \end{equation} Thus, from \eqref{eq:finance_decomposition}, \eqref{eq:optimal_v_gamma_bilinear} and \eqref{eq:radon_nykodim} we obtain \[ V^{\hat\gamma}+\log\left(\frac{d{{\hat{\mathbb Q}}}}{d\mathbb P}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\log\det(\Sigma)-\log\det(\hat Q)\right). \] Hence, from \eqref{nuetral} \begin{align} \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\left[\exp\left(-V^{\hat \gamma}\right)\right] &=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\left(\log\det(\Sigma)-\log\det(\hat Q)\right)\right) \nonumber\\ &=\exp\left(-\mathbb E_{{\hat{\mathbb Q}}}\left[\log \left(\frac{d{\hat{\mathbb Q}}}{d\mathbb P}\right)\right]\right). \end{align} Comparing \eqref{equality} with \eqref{lowerbound}, the candidate $\hat\gamma$ attains the bound that holds for every $\gamma\in\mathcal A$. Hence $\hat\gamma$ is an optimal portfolio, and the value is given by the right hand side of \eqref{eq:expected_value}. For uniqueness, equality in $xy\leq e^x+y(\log y-1)$ holds only when $x=\log y$, so any optimal $\gamma$ satisfies $-V^{\gamma}=\log\left(z^{*}\frac{d\hat{\mathbb Q}}{d\mathbb P}\right)$ almost surely. The optimal terminal wealth is therefore unique. Finally, the map $\gamma\mapsto V^{\gamma}$ is injective: conditionally on the increments before time $i$, the strategy $\gamma^i$ is deterministic and the covariance of $(X^i_1,\ldots,X^i_{p_i})$ is nondegenerate, so $V^{\gamma}=V^{\gamma'}$ almost surely forces $\gamma^i=\gamma'^i$, and backward induction on $i=N,\ldots,1$ gives $\gamma=\gamma'$. Hence the optimal portfolio is unique.

nodes.name: Bilinear triangular decomposition
nodes.statement: Given $A,{\Lambda}\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$, we seek a pair $(U,L)\in\mathcal U_n\times\mathcal L_n$ satisfying \begin{equation} {\Lambda}=L+U+UAL, \end{equation} which we call the \emph{bilinear triangular decomposition} of ${\Lambda}$.

nodes.name: Backward elimination as an analogue of LU
nodes.statement: Algorithm~\ref{alg:backward_elimination} is the natural analogue of $LU$ decomposition without pivoting, with four differences: (i)~elimination proceeds \emph{backward} (from the lower-right corner upward); (ii)~each step has one scalar pivot $\pi_k$ preceded by a triangular row-solve $M_0^{\top}u={\Lambda}_{J,k}$ with $M_0=I_{|J|}+A_{J,J}L_{J,J}$; (iii)~a zero pivot certifies non-existence of the decomposition, on an algebraic set of positive definite pairs $(A,{\Lambda})$; and (iv)~the algorithm then halts, rather than recovering by a row swap as partial pivoting does in standard $LU$.
nodes.statement_short: Like LU without pivoting, but backward, with a triangular solve and one scalar pivot per step; a zero pivot certifies non-existence.

nodes.name: Backward triangular elimination for $\Lambda=L+U+UAL$
nodes.statement: \caption{Backward triangular elimination for ${\Lambda}=L+U+UAL$} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Require $A,{\Lambda}\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$ \Ensure The unique pair $(U,L)$, or a zero-pivot certificate of nonexistence \State $U\gets\mathbf{0}_{n,n}$, \; $L\gets\mathbf{0}_{n,n}$, \; $L_{nn}\gets{\Lambda}_{nn}$ \For{$k=n-1,n-2,\ldots,1$} \State $J\gets\{k+1,\ldots,n\}$ \State $K_0\gets I_{|J|}+U_{J,J}A_{J,J}$, \; $M_0\gets I_{|J|}+A_{J,J}L_{J,J}$ \State Solve $M_0^\top u={\Lambda}_{J,k}$, \; $U_{k,J}\gets u^\top$ \State Solve $K_0\,z={\Lambda}_{J,k}$ and $K_0\,w=U_{J,J}\,A_{J,k}$ \State $\pi_k\gets 1+u^\top A_{J,k}-u^\top A_{J,J}\,w$ \If{$\pi_k=0$} \State \textbf{stop:} \eqref{eq:twisted_decomposition} has no solution \EndIf \State $L_{kk}\gets({\Lambda}_{kk}-u^\top A_{J,J}\,z)/\pi_k$, \; $L_{J,k}\gets z-w\,L_{kk}$ \EndFor \State \Return $U,L$ \end{algorithmic}
output: The unique pair $(U,L)$, or a zero-pivot certificate of nonexistence
nodes.statement_short: Eliminate backward from the lower-right corner: per step one triangular solve for the new row of $U$, one scalar pivot, and the new column of $L$; stop at a zero pivot.

nodes.name: Efficient $O(n^3)$ implementation
nodes.statement: Implemented naively, Algorithm~\ref{alg:backward_elimination} costs $O(n^4)$: lines~\ref{lin:form}--\ref{lin:solveK} build $M_0$ and $K_0$ afresh at each step and solve with them, which is $O\bigl((n-k)^3\bigr)$ work. The overall cost reduces to $O(n^3)$, matching standard LU, if those three lines are replaced by an incremental update of the two inverses $M_0^{-1}$ and $K_0^{-1}$ as $k$ decreases, followed by three matrix--vector products. Between consecutive steps the new index is prepended to the trailing block, which writes $M_0=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\tau & y^\top\\ x & M_0^{\rm prev}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ with $(M_0^{\rm prev})^{-1}$ already in hand. The Schur-complement bordering identity \[ M_0^{-1}= \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sigma & -\hat y^\top/\sigma\\[2pt] -\hat x/\sigma & (M_0^{\rm prev})^{-1}+\hat x\hat y^\top/\sigma \end{pmatrix}, \] with \[ \hat x=(M_0^{\rm prev})^{-1}x,\qquad \hat y^\top=y^\top (M_0^{\rm prev})^{-1},\qquad \sigma=\tau-y^\top\hat x, \] updates the inverse in $O\bigl((n-k)^2\bigr)$, and the analogous formula updates $K_0^{-1}$. Lines~\ref{lin:solveM} and~\ref{lin:solveK} then become the matrix--vector products $u=(M_0^{\top})^{-1}{\Lambda}_{J,k}$, $z=K_0^{-1}{\Lambda}_{J,k}$ and $w=K_0^{-1}U_{J,J}A_{J,k}$, each of cost $O\bigl((n-k)^2\bigr)$. Summing over $k$ gives $O(n^3)$.
nodes.statement_short: Update $M_0^{-1}$ and $K_0^{-1}$ by Schur-complement bordering at $O((n-k)^2)$ per step, giving $O(n^3)$ total.
nodes.label: rem:complexity

nodes.name: Proof of the regularity lemma
nodes.statement: The identity is equivalent to $(I_n+UA)L={\Lambda}-U$. Suppose $v\in\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfies $v^\top(I_n+UA)=0$. Then $v^\top({\Lambda}-U)=v^\top(I_n+UA)L=0$, so $v^\top{\Lambda}=v^\top U$. On the other hand $v^\top(I_n+UA)=0$ gives $v^\top UA=-v^\top$, and multiplying by $A^{-1}$ on the right, $v^\top U=-v^\top A^{-1}$. Combining the two identities yields $v^\top({\Lambda}+A^{-1})=0$. nodes.name: Proof of Proposition (variational form of $U$)
nodes.statement: \textbf{(i)} Set ${\Sigma}:={\Lambda}^{-1}$ and consider the $2n\times 2n$ positive definite matrix \begin{equation} B:= \begin{pmatrix} {\Sigma} & {\Sigma}\\ {\Sigma} & {\Sigma}+A \end{pmatrix}, \qquad B^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} {\Lambda}+A^{-1} & -A^{-1}\\ -A^{-1} & A^{-1} \end{pmatrix}, \end{equation} together with the subspace \[ {\mathcal S}_{2n}= \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} 0 & U\\ U^\top & 0 \end{pmatrix} :U\in\mathcal U_n \right\}\subset\mathcal M_{2n}(\mathbb{R}) \] and its orthogonal complement (with respect to the trace inner product) in the symmetric matrices, \[ {\mathcal S}_{2n}^{\perp} = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} V & L\\ L^\top & W \end{pmatrix} :V,W \text{ symmetric},\, L\in\mathcal L_n \right\}. \] Every matrix in ${\mathcal S}_{2n}$ has zero diagonal, so as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{thm:finance_value} a positive semidefinite $X\in{\mathcal S}_{2n}$ satisfies $|X_{ij}|^2\le X_{ii}X_{jj}=0$ and hence $X=0$. Thus ${\mathcal S}_{2n}\cap\mathbb S_+^{2n}=\{0\}$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:general_decomposition} applies. It therefore supplies a unique pair $(C,Q)\in{\mathcal S}_{2n}\times{\mathcal S}_{2n}^{\perp}$ such that $Q$ is positive definite and $B^{-1}=Q^{-1}+C$. Writing $C=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0 & U\\ U^\top & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, we compute \[ B^{-1}-C = \begin{pmatrix} {\Lambda}+A^{-1} & -A^{-1}-U\\ -A^{-1}-U^\top & A^{-1} \end{pmatrix}. \] The Schur complement of the $(2,2)$-block $A^{-1}$ in $B^{-1}-C$ is \begin{align*} ({\Lambda}+A^{-1}) &- (-A^{-1}-U)\,A\,(-A^{-1}-U^\top) \\ &={\Lambda}+A^{-1}-(I_n+UA)(A^{-1}+U^\top)\\ &={\Lambda}-U-U^\top-UAU^\top\;=\;S_U. \end{align*} The standard block-inverse formula then gives, for $Q=(B^{-1}-C)^{-1}$, \[ Q_{11}=S_U^{-1}, \qquad Q_{12}=-S_U^{-1}(-A^{-1}-U)\,A=S_U^{-1}(I_n+UA). \] Since $Q\in{\mathcal S}_{2n}^{\perp}$, the block $Q_{12}$ is lower triangular, and $Q\succ0$ gives $S_U=Q_{11}^{-1}\succ0$. This proves existence. For uniqueness, let $U\in\mathcal U_n$ be \emph{any} matrix with $S_U\succ0$ and $S_U^{-1}(I_n+UA)$ lower triangular, and set $C=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0 & U\\ U^\top & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\in{\mathcal S}_{2n}$. The computation above shows that $B^{-1}-C$ has $(2,2)$-block $A^{-1}\succ0$ and Schur complement $S_U\succ0$, so $B^{-1}-C\succ0$. Set $Q:=(B^{-1}-C)^{-1}\succ0$. Its blocks are again $Q_{11}=S_U^{-1}$ and $Q_{12}=S_U^{-1}(I_n+UA)$, the latter lower triangular by hypothesis, so $Q\in{\mathcal S}_{2n}^{\perp}$. Hence $(C,Q)$ is a constrained decomposition of $B^{-1}$, and the uniqueness in Theorem~\ref{thm:general_decomposition} forces it to be the one constructed above. Therefore $U$ is unique. \textbf{(ii)} For any $(U',L')\in\mathcal U_n\times\mathcal L_n$ satisfying ${\Lambda}=L'+U'+U'AL'$, a direct computation gives \begin{equation} S_{U'}=(I_n+U'A)(L'-U'^\top). \end{equation} ($\Leftarrow$) If $I_n+UA$ is invertible for the $U$ of part~\textbf{(i)}, set $L:=(I_n+UA)^{-1}({\Lambda}-U)$. Then $L-U^\top=(I_n+UA)^{-1}S_U$, and since $S_U^{-1}(I_n+UA)$ is lower triangular so is its inverse $L-U^\top$. Adding $U^\top$ yields $L\in\mathcal L_n$, so $(U,L)$ solves~\eqref{eq:twisted_decomposition} and $(A,{\Lambda})$ is regular. nodes.name: (i) Existence and uniqueness of $U$ via the $2n\times2n$ dec
nodes.statement: \textbf{(i)} Set ${\Sigma}:={\Lambda}^{-1}$ and consider the $2n\times 2n$ positive definite matrix \begin{equation} B:= \begin{pmatrix} {\Sigma} & {\Sigma}\\ {\Sigma} & {\Sigma}+A \end{pmatrix}, \qquad B^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} {\Lambda}+A^{-1} & -A^{-1}\\ -A^{-1} & A^{-1} \end{pmatrix}, \end{equation} together with the subspace \[ {\mathcal S}_{2n}= \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} 0 & U\\ U^\top & 0 \end{pmatrix} :U\in\mathcal U_n \right\}\subset\mathcal M_{2n}(\mathbb{R}) \] and its orthogonal complement (with respect to the trace inner product) in the symmetric matrices, \[ {\mathcal S}_{2n}^{\perp} = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} V & L\\ L^\top & W \end{pmatrix} :V,W \text{ symmetric},\, L\in\mathcal L_n \right\}. \] Every matrix in ${\mathcal S}_{2n}$ has zero diagonal, so as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{thm:finance_value} a positive semidefinite $X\in{\mathcal S}_{2n}$ satisfies $|X_{ij}|^2\le X_{ii}X_{jj}=0$ and hence $X=0$. Thus ${\mathcal S}_{2n}\cap\mathbb S_+^{2n}=\{0\}$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:general_decomposition} applies. It therefore supplies a unique pair $(C,Q)\in{\mathcal S}_{2n}\times{\mathcal S}_{2n}^{\perp}$ such that $Q$ is positive definite and $B^{-1}=Q^{-1}+C$. Writing $C=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0 & U\\ U^\top & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, we compute \[ B^{-1}-C = \begin{pmatrix} {\Lambda}+A^{-1} & -A^{-1}-U\\ -A^{-1}-U^\top & A^{-1} \end{pmatrix}. \] The Schur complement of the $(2,2)$-block $A^{-1}$ in $B^{-1}-C$ is \begin{align*} ({\Lambda}+A^{-1}) &- (-A^{-1}-U)\,A\,(-A^{-1}-U^\top) \\ &={\Lambda}+A^{-1}-(I_n+UA)(A^{-1}+U^\top)\\ &={\Lambda}-U-U^\top-UAU^\top\;=\;S_U. \end{align*} The standard block-inverse formula then gives, for $Q=(B^{-1}-C)^{-1}$, \[ Q_{11}=S_U^{-1}, \qquad Q_{12}=-S_U^{-1}(-A^{-1}-U)\,A=S_U^{-1}(I_n+UA). \] Since $Q\in{\mathcal S}_{2n}^{\perp}$, the block $Q_{12}$ is lower triangular, and $Q\succ0$ gives $S_U=Q_{11}^{-1}\succ0$. This proves existence. For uniqueness, let $U\in\mathcal U_n$ be \emph{any} matrix with $S_U\succ0$ and $S_U^{-1}(I_n+UA)$ lower triangular, and set $C=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0 & U\\ U^\top & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\in{\mathcal S}_{2n}$. The computation above shows that $B^{-1}-C$ has $(2,2)$-block $A^{-1}\succ0$ and Schur complement $S_U\succ0$, so $B^{-1}-C\succ0$. Set $Q:=(B^{-1}-C)^{-1}\succ0$. Its blocks are again $Q_{11}=S_U^{-1}$ and $Q_{12}=S_U^{-1}(I_n+UA)$, the latter lower triangular by hypothesis, so $Q\in{\mathcal S}_{2n}^{\perp}$. Hence $(C,Q)$ is a constrained decomposition of $B^{-1}$, and the uniqueness in Theorem~\ref{thm:general_decomposition} forces it to be the one constructed above. Therefore $U$ is unique.
nodes.statement_short: (i) Existence and uniqueness of $U$ via the $2n\times2n$ decomposition

nodes.name: The $2\times2$ case
nodes.statement: Write $A=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ and ${\Lambda}=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}p&q\\q&r\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, and $U=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0 & u\\ 0 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$. Running Algorithm~\ref{alg:backward_elimination}: $L_{22}=r$, then $M_0=1+cr>0$ and $u=q/(1+cr)$, so \[ U=\begin{pmatrix}0 & q/(1+cr)\\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}. \] The pivot is $\pi_1=1+ub=(1+cr+bq)/(1+cr)$, which equals $\det(I_n+UA)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:triangular_decomposition}\textbf{(ii)} the bilinear triangular decomposition exists if and only if \[ 1+cr+bq\neq 0, \] in which case \[ L=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{(1+cr)p-cq^2}{1+cr+bq} & 0\\[6pt] q & r\end{pmatrix}. \] For $A=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}2 & -1\\ -1 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ and ${\Lambda}=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}5 & 2\\ 2 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ (both positive definite with $\det A=\det{\Lambda}=1$), $1+cr+bq=1+1-2=0$, so the bilinear triangular decomposition does not exist. nodes.name: The role of $A$
nodes.statement: If $A$ is diagonal, then $(A,{\Lambda})$ is triangularly regular for every positive definite ${\Lambda}$: the product $UA$ is then strictly upper triangular, so $I_n+UA$ is unipotent upper triangular and hence invertible, and Proposition~\ref{prop:variational_U}\textbf{(ii)} applies. nodes.statement_short: For diagonal $A$ every pair is triangularly regular; for non-diagonal $A$ regularity can fail.
nodes.label: rem:good_A

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition (local stability)
nodes.statement: Let $A_t:=A+t\Delta=(1-t)A+t\widetilde A$ for $t\in[0,1]$. Both $A$ and $\widetilde A$ lie in $\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$, which is convex, so $A_t\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:general_decomposition} supplies a decomposition $(B_t,C_t)$ of $A_t$; thus $(B_0,C_0)=(B^{*},C^{*})$ and $(B_1,C_1)=(\widetilde B,\widetilde C)$. Consider the optimality map $F(A,C):=\mathrm{proj}_{\mathcal{S}}\big((A-C)^{-1}\big)\in {\mathcal{S}}$, where $\mathrm{proj}_{\mathcal{S}}$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbb{S}^n$ onto ${\mathcal{S}}$, so that $F(A_t,C_t)=0$ is the first-order condition $\mathrm{tr}\bigl((A_t-C_t)^{-1}X\bigr)=0$ for all $X\in {\mathcal{S}}$. \emph{Step 1 (differentiate along the path).} Since $\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=0}(M+sE)^{-1}=-M^{-1}EM^{-1}$, differentiating $F$ in each argument gives, for $(\Delta,X)\in\mathbb{S}^n\times {\mathcal{S}}$, \begin{align} \frac{d}{ds}\Big|_{s=0}F(A_t,C_t+sX)&=\mathrm{proj}_{\mathcal{S}}(B_tXB_t),\notag\\ \frac{d}{ds}\Big|_{s=0}F(A_t+s\Delta,C_t)&=-\mathrm{proj}_{\mathcal{S}}(B_t\Delta B_t). \end{align} By the definition of $\alpha$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha_lipschitz}\textbf{(i)}, every $X\in {\mathcal{S}}\setminus\{0\}$ satisfies \[ \langle\mathrm{proj}_{\mathcal{S}}(B_tXB_t),X\rangle_F=\mathrm{tr}(B_tXB_tX)\ge\alpha(B_t,{\mathcal{S}})\|X\|_F^2>0 , \] so the linear map $X\mapsto\mathrm{proj}_{\mathcal{S}}(B_tXB_t)$ is injective on the finite-dimensional space ${\mathcal{S}}$, hence bijective. Matrix inversion is real analytic on the invertible matrices, so $F$ is real analytic, and with this invertibility the analytic implicit function theorem applies: near every $A_t$ it produces a real-analytic map solving $F(A,\cdot)=0$, which by the uniqueness in Theorem~\ref{thm:general_decomposition} is $A\mapsto C^{*}(A)$. Hence $t\mapsto C_t$ is real analytic, as is $t\mapsto B_t=(A_t-C_t)^{-1}$. Write $\dot C_t:=\frac{d}{dt}C_t$ and $\dot B_t:=\frac{d}{dt}B_t$. Since every $C_t$ lies in the subspace ${\mathcal{S}}$, so does $\dot C_t$. By the chain rule and~\eqref{eq:dF}, differentiating $F(A_t,C_t)=0$ in $t$ gives \begin{equation} \mathrm{proj}_{\mathcal{S}}\big(B_t\,\dot C_t\,B_t\big)=\mathrm{proj}_{\mathcal{S}}(B_t\Delta B_t). \end{equation} \emph{Step 2 (the derivative is a projection).} For $B\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$ the formula \begin{equation} \langle X,Y\rangle_B:=\mathrm{tr}(BXBY),\qquad \|X\|_B:=\sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(BXBX)} , \end{equation} defines an inner product on $\mathbb{S}^n$. It is bilinear and symmetric, and $\langle X,X\rangle_B=\|B^{1/2}XB^{1/2}\|_F^2$ vanishes only for $X=0$, since $B^{1/2}$ is invertible. Pairing~\eqref{eq:dC_eq} with $X\in {\mathcal{S}}$ and using $\langle\mathrm{proj}_{\mathcal{S}}(Y),X\rangle_F=\langle Y,X\rangle_F$ for $Y\in\mathbb{S}^n$ shows that $\langle \dot C_t,X\rangle_{B_t}=\langle\Delta,X\rangle_{B_t}$ for every $X\in {\mathcal{S}}$. Since $\dot C_t$ itself lies in ${\mathcal{S}}$, this identifies $\dot C_t$ as the orthogonal projection of $\Delta$ onto ${\mathcal{S}}$ in the inner product~\eqref{eq:B_inner}. Set $R_t:=\Delta-\dot C_t$. Orthogonality gives $\|\Delta\|_{B_t}^2=\|\dot C_t\|_{B_t}^2+\|R_t\|_{B_t}^2$, so $\|\dot C_t\|_{B_t}\le\|\Delta\|_{B_t}$ and $\|R_t\|_{B_t}\le\|\Delta\|_{B_t}$. By~\eqref{eq:alpha_def_fro}, $\sqrt{\alpha(B_t,{\mathcal{S}})}\|X\|_F\le\|X\|_{B_t}$ for $X\in {\mathcal{S}}$, while $\|\Delta\|_{B_t}=\|B_t^{1/2}\Delta B_t^{1/2}\|_F\le\|B_t\|_2\,\delta$, where $\delta:=\|\Delta\|_F$. Combining, \begin{equation} \|\dot C_t\|_F\le\frac{\|B_t\|_2}{\sqrt{\alpha(B_t,{\mathcal{S}})}}\,\delta =\kappa(B_t,{\mathcal{S}})\,\delta . \end{equation} Differentiating $B_t=(A_t-C_t)^{-1}$ gives $\dot B_t=-B_tR_tB_t$, and writing $W:=B_t^{1/2}R_tB_t^{1/2}$, so that $B_tR_tB_t=B_t^{1/2}WB_t^{1/2}$, yields \begin{align} \|\dot B_t\|_2&\le\|B_t\|_2\|W\|_2\le\|B_t\|_2\|W\|_F =\|B_t\|_2\|R_t\|_{B_t}\notag\\ &\le\|B_t\|_2\|\Delta\|_{B_t}\le\|B_t\|_2^2\,\delta . \end{align} \emph{Step 3 (integrate).} Recall from Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha_lipschitz}\textbf{(i)} that $\alpha(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})\le\|B^{*}\|_2^2$, equivalently $\kappa(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})\ge1$. The coefficients in~\eqref{eq:dC_bound} and~\eqref{eq:dB_bound} are evaluated at the intermediate decomposition $B_t$, which is unknown, whereas the statement involves only $B_0=B^{*}$. We therefore first bound $\|B_t\|_2$ in terms of $\|B^{*}\|_2$. Since $t\mapsto B_t$ is continuously differentiable on the compact interval $[0,1]$, the map $t\mapsto\|B_t\|_2$ is Lipschitz and hence absolutely continuous, and by~\eqref{eq:dB_bound} it satisfies $\frac{d}{dt}\|B_t\|_2\le\|\dot B_t\|_2\le\delta\,\|B_t\|_2^2$ for almost every $t$. Therefore, by the chain rule, $\frac{d}{dt}\|B_t\|_2^{-1}\ge-\delta$ almost everywhere, and integrating from $0$ gives $\|B_t\|_2^{-1}\ge\|B^{*}\|_2^{-1}-\delta t$. Hence, whenever $\|B^{*}\|_2\,\delta<1$, \begin{equation} \|B_t\|_2\le\frac{\|B^{*}\|_2}{1-\|B^{*}\|_2\,\delta t},\qquad 0\le t\le 1. \end{equation} By~\eqref{eq:smallness_fro} and $\kappa(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})\ge1$ we have $\|B^{*}\|_2\,\delta=\varepsilon/\kappa(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})^2\le\varepsilon$. Therefore~\eqref{eq:B_comparison} gives $\|B_t\|_2\le\|B^{*}\|_2/(1-\varepsilon)$ for all $t\in[0,1]$, and \begin{align*} \|B_t-B^{*}\|_2&\le\int_0^t\delta\,\|B_s\|_2^2\,ds \le\int_0^t\frac{\delta\,\|B^{*}\|_2^2}{\big(1-\|B^{*}\|_2\,\delta s\big)^2}\,ds\\ &=\frac{\|B^{*}\|_2^2\,\delta t}{1-\|B^{*}\|_2\,\delta t} \le\frac{\|B^{*}\|_2^2\,\delta}{1-\|B^{*}\|_2\,\delta}\le\frac{\|B^{*}\|_2^2\,\delta}{1-\varepsilon} , \end{align*} At $t=1$ the first bound is~\eqref{eq:B_stab_fro}. Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha_lipschitz}\textbf{(ii)} bounds the drift of $\alpha$, and~\eqref{eq:smallness_fro} in the form $\|B^{*}\|_2^3\,\delta=\varepsilon\,\alpha(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})$ turns it into a fraction of $\alpha(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})$, \[ \big|\alpha(B_t,{\mathcal{S}})-\alpha(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})\big| \le\big(\|B_t\|_2+\|B^{*}\|_2\big)\|B_t-B^{*}\|_2 \le\frac{\varepsilon(2-\varepsilon)}{(1-\varepsilon)^2}\,\alpha(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}}) . \] Since $(1-\varepsilon)^2-\varepsilon(2-\varepsilon)=1-4\varepsilon+2\varepsilon^2$, positive by the hypothesis on $\varepsilon$, this gives $\alpha(B_t,{\mathcal{S}})\ge(1-4\varepsilon+2\varepsilon^{2})(1-\varepsilon)^{-2} \alpha(B^{*},{\mathcal{S}})$ throughout. nodes.statement: \emph{Step 1 (differentiate along the path).} Since $\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=0}(M+sE)^{-1}=-M^{-1}EM^{-1}$, differentiating $F$ in each argument gives, for $(\Delta,X)\in\mathbb{S}^n\times {\mathcal{S}}$, \begin{align} \frac{d}{ds}\Big|_{s=0}F(A_t,C_t+sX)&=\mathrm{proj}_{\mathcal{S}}(B_tXB_t),\notag\\ \frac{d}{ds}\Big|_{s=0}F(A_t+s\Delta,C_t)&=-\mathrm{proj}_{\mathcal{S}}(B_t\Delta B_t). \end{align} By the definition of $\alpha$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha_lipschitz}\textbf{(i)}, every $X\in {\mathcal{S}}\setminus\{0\}$ satisfies \[ \langle\mathrm{proj}_{\mathcal{S}}(B_tXB_t),X\rangle_F=\mathrm{tr}(B_tXB_tX)\ge\alpha(B_t,{\mathcal{S}})\|X\|_F^2>0 , \] so the linear map $X\mapsto\mathrm{proj}_{\mathcal{S}}(B_tXB_t)$ is injective on the finite-dimensional space ${\mathcal{S}}$, hence bijective. nodes.statement: \emph{Step 2 (the derivative is a projection).} For $B\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}$ the formula \begin{equation} \langle X,Y\rangle_B:=\mathrm{tr}(BXBY),\qquad \|X\|_B:=\sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(BXBX)} , \end{equation} defines an inner product on $\mathbb{S}^n$. nodes.statement: (dense, small ${\mathcal{S}}$, Newton-CG): the setting of Example~I solved by Newton-CG rather than exact Newton.
